newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK inflation seen steady in November.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK inflation seen steady in November.

text.p: UK underlying inflation is set to stick stubbornly at 3.3 percent in November as firmer prices for household goods and clothing offset the downward effect of softer seasonal food prices, economists said.
The Reuter poll forecasts retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments rose 3.3 percent in the year to November, unchanged from October. The data are due at 0930 GMT on Thursday.
"On the food front, (1996) is akin to 1993 with the supermarkets competing aggressively on price," said Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets.
This should continue into November, which also generally benefits from seasonal offers on alcohol.
"But household goods and clothing prices usually firm before Christmas and motoring costs are still rising," he said.
Dicks calculates this could add 0.1 percent on to the monthly measure of headline retail prices, but leaving the year-on-year measure also unchanged at 2.7 percent.

Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, forecast the lower cost of food, largely a function of the stronger pound, could actually help underlying inflation edge down to 3.2 percent in November.
"Upstream food prices have fallen and should soon feed through to supermarkets. This is a very important factor and will allow RPI to fall sharply in coming months."
Overall, producer prices have eased during 1996. Output prices were unchanged in November and core prices were up 0.8 percent year-on-year, the lowest core rate of increase for almost 30 years.
However, Barr said there were some upside risks in the November data.
"Although upstream petrol prices have peaked, a survey of (petrol retailers) showed they actually rose further on the forecourts in November."
And there is a danger that retailers will take advantage of strong consumer demand to rebuild their margins, badly damaged by the downturn in 1995.

"Consumers have been quite price conscious until now and retailers have pandered to that. But it is quite possible that in the run up to Christmas they will be able to squeeze through higher prices," said Peter Osler, UK economist at GNI.

Underlying inflation picked up to 3.3 percent in the year to October versus 2.9 percent in September, sending gilts and short sterling into a tailspin as fears mounted that interest rates would rise sharply.
But many economists say the stronger pound, up around 10 percent on a trade-weighted basis from August levels, will help push down prices overall as import prices cheapen.
"Inflation will probably ease in the short-term, but the last few months has been disappointing and it doesn't look like the government is going to hit its target," said Osler.
The government has set a medium-term target of 2.5 percent for underlying inflation.
